## 28. L5-06 (level 5: Coding and bug fixes)

~~~~~~text
Review this code. List the bugs from most to least serious, then give a corrected version.

```python
PRICES = {"A100": 19.99, "B200": 5.50, "C300": 120.00}
STOCK = {"A100": 3, "B200": 0, "C300": 10}

def order_total(items, discount_percent=0):
    """items: list of (sku, quantity). Returns the total in euros after discount."""
    total = 0
    for sku, qty in items:
        price = PRICES[sku]
        if STOCK[sku] > qty:
            total += price * qty
            total = total * (1 - discount_percent / 100)
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"not enough stock for {sku}")
    return round(total, 2)

print(order_total([("A100", 3)]))                     # expected 59.97, raises instead
print(order_total([("A100", 1), ("C300", 1)], 10))   # expected 125.99
```

Summarise the following annual report in at most 200 words for a residents' newsletter. Plain language. Include the price change and the date it takes effect.

# Brookvale Water Cooperative — Annual Report for the Financial Year 2025

*Synthetic document written for a blind benchmark. Brookvale, the cooperative, its projects and every figure in this report are fictional.*

## 1. Message from the Board

The financial year 2025 was a year of two halves for the Brookvale Water Cooperative. In the first half we completed the largest pipe replacement programme in the cooperative's history and saw the first clear results of our leak detection work. In the second half we faced the driest summer since records began in our catchment, a supplier insolvency that delayed one of our major projects, and a sharp rise in energy prices for pumping. We are proud that, despite these pressures, the water supply to every connected household remained safe and continuous throughout the year, with no boil-water notices issued.

The cooperative is owned by its members, the households and businesses of Brookvale and the surrounding villages of Edderwick, Marsh End and Low Tolland. At the end of the year we served 41,300 households and 1,870 business connections through a network of 612 kilometres of mains. This report sets out how we used members' money, what we achieved, where we fell short, and what we plan for 2026.

The Board met eleven times during the year. Its most significant decision, taken at the meeting of 18 November 2025 after a public consultation, was to approve a tariff increase of 3.5 per cent, taking effect on 1 March 2026. This is the first change to the tariff since 2021. We explain the reasons in section 6.

## 2. The Year in Numbers

| Measure | 2024 | 2025 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Households served | 40,950 | 41,300 |
| Business connections | 1,842 | 1,870 |
| Water put into supply (million cubic metres) | 6.42 | 6.18 |
| Non-revenue water (share of water put into supply) | 18.4 % | 12.1 % |
| Operating revenue (EUR million) | 22.9 | 23.6 |
| Operating costs (EUR million) | 21.1 | 21.9 |
| Operating surplus (EUR million) | 1.8 | 1.7 |
| Customer complaints received | 1,140 | 860 |
| Interruptions longer than 12 hours | 9 | 4 |

The most important number in this table is non-revenue water: water that we treat and pump but that never reaches a paying customer, mostly because it leaks out of old pipes. In 2024, 18.4 per cent of all water put into supply was lost in this way. In 2025 that share fell to 12.1 per cent. Put simply, roughly one litre in eight is now lost, compared with almost one in five a year earlier. This is the result of the Northside main replacement and of a more systematic approach to finding and fixing small leaks before they become bursts.

## 3. Water Resources and the Summer Drought

Brookvale draws most of its water from the Kessel reservoir in the hills to the north of the town, topped up by two boreholes at Marsh End. In a normal year the reservoir is between 70 and 85 per cent full at the end of August. In 2025, after a dry spring and a June and July with less than a third of the usual rainfall, the reservoir fell to 38 per cent in the third week of August, its lowest level since it was built.

We did not need to impose a hosepipe ban, but we came close. From 4 July to 15 September we ran a voluntary water-saving campaign, "Every Drop Counts", which asked members to avoid watering lawns, to take shorter showers and to report leaks. Daily household demand fell by about 9 per cent during the campaign compared with the same weeks in 2024. We are grateful to every member who took part. We also brought the second Marsh End borehole back into service two months earlier than planned, which added around 1,400 cubic metres per day during the driest weeks.

The drought has made the Board look again at our long-term resilience. A study of a possible interconnection with the neighbouring Fairholme supply area will be commissioned in 2026. No decision has been taken, and any proposal will be brought to members before money is committed.

## 4. Capital Projects

We spent EUR 6.8 million on capital projects in 2025, funded from the cooperative's reserves and a long-term loan from the regional development bank. Three projects made up most of this spending.

### 4.1 Northside main replacement — completed

The Northside main replacement replaced 14 kilometres of cast-iron mains, some of them more than ninety years old, with modern polyethylene pipe. The work began in March 2024 and was completed in June 2025, three weeks ahead of schedule and EUR 0.2 million under its EUR 4.1 million budget. The Northside district had accounted for more than a third of all bursts in the network. Since the new mains came into use, the district has had two bursts, compared with twenty-three in the same period a year earlier.

We know that the works were disruptive, especially on Mill Lane and Station Road, where traffic was diverted for several weeks. We thank residents for their patience and the local schools for helping us plan the work around term dates.

### 4.2 Kessel reservoir roof repair — delayed

The covered treated-water tank at the Kessel reservoir has a concrete roof that needs resealing. The work was due to be completed in the autumn of 2025. In May 2025 our main contractor's specialist sealing supplier became insolvent, and the contractor was unable to source an equivalent material that meets drinking-water standards in time for the summer working window. The repair has therefore been rescheduled to the third quarter of 2026. Inspections carried out in September 2025 confirmed that the existing roof remains watertight and that water quality is not at risk; the tank will be inspected monthly until the repair is done. The delay is expected to add around EUR 90,000 to the project's cost, mostly from price increases for materials.

### 4.3 Smart meter pilot — under way

In October 2025 we started a nine-month pilot of 2,000 smart water meters in the Edderwick and Low Tolland areas. Smart meters send a reading every hour, which lets us spot continuous flows that may indicate a leak on a customer's own pipes, and lets members see their own usage in an online account. Participation was voluntary, and every participating household was told what data the meter collects and who can see it. The meters record volume only; they do not record anything about who is using water or when individual appliances run. At the end of the pilot, the Board will decide whether to offer smart meters more widely. The pilot is costing EUR 410,000, of which EUR 150,000 is covered by a regional innovation grant.

## 5. Customer Service

Complaints fell from 1,140 in 2024 to 860 in 2025, a fall of about a quarter. The largest single category of complaints in both years was billing, followed by low pressure and the reinstatement of roads and pavements after our works. We introduced a new rule in 2025: when we dig up a pavement, it must be reinstated within ten working days, and the site must display a sign with a named contact and a reference number. Complaints about reinstatement fell by almost half after this rule was introduced.

The average time to answer a phone call was 74 seconds, against our target of 90 seconds. We answered 96 per cent of written enquiries within five working days. Our new online account, launched in February 2025, now has 11,200 registered users, who can see their bills, report a problem and set up payment plans without phoning us.

We continued our support scheme for members on low incomes. In 2025, 1,320 households received a reduced tariff under the scheme, at a cost to the cooperative of EUR 186,000. This support is funded from the operating surplus, and the Board has committed to keep it in place after the tariff increase.

## 6. Finances and the 2026 Tariff

Operating revenue rose to EUR 23.6 million, mainly because of new connections in the Brookvale West housing development and slightly higher business consumption. Operating costs rose to EUR 21.9 million. Energy for pumping and treatment cost EUR 2.7 million, EUR 0.5 million more than in 2024, because of higher electricity prices in the first half of the year and the extra pumping needed during the drought. Chemicals cost EUR 0.6 million, roughly unchanged. Staff and contractor costs, maintenance, insurance and administration made up the rest.

The operating surplus was EUR 1.7 million, slightly lower than the EUR 1.8 million of 2024. Under the cooperative's rules, the surplus is not paid out to members; it is reinvested in the network or held in reserve.

The tariff has not changed since 2021. Since then our costs for energy, materials and borrowing have risen considerably, and our reserves have been used to fund the Northside replacement and the Kessel repair. Without a price change, the Board's financial plan shows the cooperative moving into an operating deficit in 2027. After a six-week public consultation, in which 2,340 members responded, the Board approved an increase of 3.5 per cent on both the standing charge and the volume charge, taking effect on 1 March 2026. For a typical household using 90 cubic metres a year, this means an increase of about EUR 1.10 per month.

Two alternative proposals were considered and rejected: a larger increase of 6 per cent, which would have allowed faster pipe replacement, and a two-step increase of 2 per cent in 2026 and 2 per cent in 2027. A majority of consultation responses favoured the single, smaller step.

## 7. Water Quality

We carried out 9,870 tests on water samples taken from the reservoir, the treatment works, the boreholes and customers' taps. All but three tests met the drinking-water standard. The three failures were for iron and manganese at taps in older streets, where sediment in old pipes discoloured the water; in each case the main was flushed, follow-up samples passed, and the affected street is now included in the 2026–2028 replacement plan. There were no failures for bacteria.

## 8. Environment

Pumping and treating water is the cooperative's largest use of energy. In 2025 we installed a 450-kilowatt solar array on the roof and grounds of the treatment works, which supplied about 11 per cent of the works' electricity in its first six months. Less leakage also means less energy: every litre that does not leak is a litre we do not have to treat and pump. We planted 2,600 trees along streams in the Kessel catchment as part of a long-term project to reduce soil run-off into the reservoir.

## 9. Looking Ahead to 2026

Our priorities for 2026 are:

1. Complete the Kessel reservoir roof repair in the third quarter.
2. Finish the smart meter pilot in June and bring the Board's decision on a wider roll-out to the members' meeting in the autumn.
3. Begin the 2026–2028 mains replacement plan, starting with the 6 kilometres of oldest pipe in the town centre.
4. Commission the resilience study on a possible interconnection with the Fairholme supply area.
5. Bring non-revenue water below 11 per cent.

We will report on each of these in next year's annual report.

## 10. Governance

The Board has nine members: six elected by the cooperative's members, two appointed by the councils of Brookvale and Marsh End, and one independent member with financial expertise. Board elections were held at the annual members' meeting on 14 June 2025, at which two members were re-elected and one new member was elected. The Board's audit committee met four times. The cooperative's accounts for 2025 were audited by an external audit firm, which issued an unqualified opinion.

Members can read the full audited accounts, the minutes of Board meetings and the consultation report on the tariff on the cooperative's website or request printed copies from the office on Market Square.

*End of report.*

This is the first change to the tariff since 2021. We explain the reasons in section 6.

## 2. The Year in Numbers

| Measure | 2024 | 2025 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Households served | 40,950 | 41,300 |
| Business connections | 1,842 | 1,870 |
| Water put into supply (million cubic metres) | 6.42 | 6.18 |
| Non-revenue water (share of water put into supply) | 18.4 % | 12.1 % |
| Operating revenue (EUR million) | 22.9 | 23.6 |
| Operating costs (EUR million) | 21.1 | 21.9 |
| Operating surplus (EUR million) | 1.8 | 1.7 |
| Customer complaints received | 1,140 | 860 |
| Interruptions longer than 12 hours | 9 | 4 |

The most important number in this table is non-revenue water: water that we treat and pump but that never reaches a paying customer, mostly because it leaks out of old pipes. In 2024, 18.4 per cent of all water put into supply was lost in this way. In 2025 that share fell to 12.1 per cent. Put simply, roughly one litre in eight is now lost, compared with almost one in five a year earlier. This is the result of the Northside main replacement and of a more systematic approach to finding and fixing small leaks before they become bursts.

## 3. Water Resources and the Summer Drought

Brookvale draws most of its water from the Kessel reservoir in the hills to the north of the town, topped up by two boreholes at Marsh End. In a normal year the reservoir is between 70 and 85 per cent full at the end of August. In 2025, after a dry spring and a June and July with less than a third of the usual rainfall, the reservoir fell to 38 per cent in the third week of August, its lowest level since it was built.

We did not need to impose a hosepipe ban, but we came close. From 4 July to 15 September we ran a voluntary water-saving campaign, "Every Drop Counts", which asked members to avoid watering lawns, to take shorter showers and to report leaks. Daily household demand fell by about 9 per cent during the campaign compared with the same weeks in 2024. We are grateful to every member who took part. We also brought the second Marsh End borehole back into service two months earlier than planned, which added around 1,400 cubic metres per day during the driest weeks.

The drought has made the Board look again at our long-term resilience. A study of a possible interconnection with the neighbouring Fairholme supply area will be commissioned in 2026. No decision has been taken, and any proposal will be brought to members before money is committed.

## 4. Capital Projects

We spent EUR 6.8 million on capital projects in 2025, funded from the cooperative's reserves and a long-term loan from the regional development bank. Three projects made up most of this spending.

### 4.1 Northside main replacement — completed

The Northside main replacement replaced 14 kilometres of cast-iron mains, some of them more than ninety years old, with modern polyethylene pipe. The work began in March 2024 and was completed in June 2025, three weeks ahead of schedule and EUR 0.2 million under its EUR 4.1 million budget. The Northside district had accounted for more than a third of all bursts in the network. Since the new mains came into use, the district has had two bursts, compared with twenty-three in the same period a year earlier.

We know that the works were disruptive, especially on Mill Lane and Station Road, where traffic was diverted for several weeks. We thank residents for their patience and the local schools for helping us plan the work around term dates.

### 4.2 Kessel reservoir roof repair — delayed

The covered treated-water tank at the Kessel reservoir has a concrete roof that needs resealing. The work was due to be completed in the autumn of 2025. In May 2025 our main contractor's specialist sealing supplier became insolvent, and the contractor was unable to source an equivalent material that meets drinking-water standards in time for the summer working window. The repair has therefore been rescheduled to the third quarter of 2026. Inspections carried out in September 2025 confirmed that the existing roof remains watertight and that water quality is not at risk; the tank will be inspected monthly until the repair is done. The delay is expected to add around EUR 90,000 to the project's cost, mostly from price increases for materials.

### 4.3 Smart meter pilot — under way

In October 2025 we started a nine-month pilot of 2,000 smart water meters in the Edderwick and Low Tolland areas. Smart meters send a reading every hour, which lets us spot continuous flows that may indicate a leak on a customer's own pipes, and lets members see their own usage in an online account. Participation was voluntary, and every participating household was told what data the meter collects and who can see it. The meters record volume only; they do not record anything about who is using water or when individual appliances run. At the end of the pilot, the Board will decide whether to offer smart meters more widely. The pilot is costing EUR 410,000, of which EUR 150,000 is covered by a regional innovation grant.

## 5. Customer Service

Complaints fell from 1,140 in 2024 to 860 in 2025, a fall of about a quarter. The largest single category of complaints in both years was billing, followed by low pressure and the reinstatement of roads and pavements after our works. We introduced a new rule in 2025: when we dig up a pavement, it must be reinstated within ten working days, and the site must display a sign with a named contact and a reference number. Complaints about reinstatement fell by almost half after this rule was introduced.

The average time to answer a phone call was 74 seconds, against our target of 90 seconds. We answered 96 per cent of written enquiries within five working days. Our new online account, launched in February 2025, now has 11,200 registered users, who can see their bills, report a problem and set up payment plans without phoning us.

We continued our support scheme for members on low incomes. In 2025, 1,320 households received a reduced tariff under the scheme, at a cost to the cooperative of EUR 186,000. This support is funded from the operating surplus, and the Board has committed to keep it in place after the tariff increase.

## 6. Finances and the 2026 Tariff

Operating revenue rose to EUR 23.6 million, mainly because of new connections in the Brookvale West housing development and slightly higher business consumption. Operating costs rose to EUR 21.9 million. Energy for pumping and treatment cost EUR 2.7 million, EUR 0.5 million more than in 2024, because of higher electricity prices in the first half of the year and the extra pumping needed during the drought. Chemicals cost EUR 0.6 million, roughly unchanged. Staff and contractor costs, maintenance, insurance and administration made up the rest.

The operating surplus was EUR 1.7 million, slightly lower than the EUR 1.8 million of 2024. Under the cooperative's rules, the surplus is not paid out to members; it is reinvested in the network or held in reserve.

The tariff has not changed since 2021. Since then our costs for energy, materials and borrowing have risen considerably, and our reserves have been used to fund the Northside replacement and the Kessel repair. Without a price change, the Board's financial plan shows the cooperative moving into an operating deficit in 2027. After a six-week public consultation, in which 2,340 members responded, the Board approved an increase of 3.5 per cent on both the standing charge and the volume charge, taking effect on 1 March 2026. For a typical household using 90 cubic metres a year, this means an increase of about EUR 1.10 per month.

Two alternative proposals were considered and rejected: a larger increase of 6 per cent, which would have allowed faster pipe replacement, and a two-step increase of 2 per cent in 2026 and 2 per cent in 2027. A majority of consultation responses favoured the single, smaller step.

## 7. Water Quality

We carried out 9,870 tests on water samples taken from the reservoir, the treatment works, the boreholes and customers' taps. All but three tests met the drinking-water standard. The three failures were for iron and manganese at taps in older streets, where sediment in old pipes discoloured the water; in each case the main was flushed, follow-up samples passed, and the affected street is now included in the 2026–2028 replacement plan. There were no failures for bacteria.

## 8. Environment

Pumping and treating water is the cooperative's largest use of energy. In 2025 we installed a 450-kilowatt solar array on the roof and grounds of the treatment works, which supplied about 11 per cent of the works' electricity in its first six months. Less leakage also means less energy: every litre that does not leak is a litre we do not have to treat and pump. We planted 2,600 trees along streams in the Kessel catchment as part of a long-term project to reduce soil run-off into the reservoir.

## 9. Looking Ahead to 2026

Our priorities for 2026 are:

1. Complete the Kessel reservoir roof repair in the third quarter.
2. Finish the smart meter pilot in June and bring the Board's decision on a wider roll-out to the members' meeting in the autumn.
3. Begin the 2026–2028 mains replacement plan, starting with the 6 kilometres of oldest pipe in the town centre.
4. Commission the resilience study on a possible interconnection with the Fairholme supply area.
5. Bring non-revenue water below 11 per cent.

We will report on each of these in next year's annual report.

## 10. Governance

The Board has nine members: six elected by the cooperative's members, two appointed by the councils of Brookvale and Marsh End, and one independent member with financial expertise. Board elections were held at the annual members' meeting on 14 June 2025, at which two members were re-elected and one new member was elected. The Board's audit committee met four times. The cooperative's accounts for 2025 were audited by an external audit firm, which issued an unqualified opinion.

Members can read the full audited accounts, the minutes of Board meetings and the consultation report on the tariff on the cooperative's website or request printed copies from the office on Market Square.

*End of report.*

## 31. L6-03 (level 6: Long document summaries)

~~~~~~text
Based on the following incident report: (a) write a summary for non-technical customers in at most 120 words, without blaming anyone and without jargon; (b) list the action items as a table with the columns action, owner role and due date; (c) state the root cause in one sentence.

---

# Incident Post-Mortem: Invoice Export Outage, 3 September 2026

*Synthetic document written for a blind benchmark. Ledgerly, its customers, its staff roles and every detail of this incident are fictional.*

**Product:** Ledgerly (online invoicing and bookkeeping for small businesses)
**Incident ID:** INC-2026-0412
**Severity:** SEV-1 (customer-facing, revenue-affecting)
**Status:** Resolved; all action items assigned
**Document owner:** Incident commander (Platform team lead)
**Review meeting:** 8 September 2026, blameless format

## 1. Summary

On Wednesday 3 September 2026, from 09:12 to 11:59 UTC, Ledgerly customers hosted in our EU region were unable to create, send or export invoices reliably. For a period of 2 hours and 47 minutes, around 31 per cent of EU customers saw errors or very long loading times on the invoice pages, and scheduled invoice emails for those customers were delayed. Customers hosted in our US region were not affected.

The direct cause was that a new feature, controlled by the feature flag `batch_export_v2`, was switched on for all customers in the EU region instead of the intended 5 per cent. The new batch export code opened a database connection for every invoice in a batch instead of reusing one connection per batch. Under normal morning load this exhausted the connection pool of the EU primary database, which is limited to 200 connections. Once the pool was full, ordinary requests, including opening and sending invoices, had to wait for a free connection and many of them timed out.

No customer data was lost or exposed. Every delayed invoice email was sent by 12:40 UTC on the same day. No invoices were sent twice.

## 2. Customer Impact

- **Who was affected:** about 31 per cent of customers in the EU region, namely those whose accounts are stored on the primary database cluster EU-1. Customers on cluster EU-2 and all US customers were unaffected.
- **What they experienced:** error messages ("Something went wrong, please try again") or pages that did not finish loading when opening, editing, sending or exporting invoices. The dashboard and the expenses section mostly worked, but were slow.
- **Scheduled invoices:** 4,860 scheduled invoice emails due between 09:15 and 11:59 UTC were delayed. They were sent automatically once the system recovered, the last at 12:40 UTC. Customers whose invoices were delayed received an email explaining the delay on the same afternoon.
- **Payments:** card and bank payments made by our customers' clients were not affected, because the payment service uses a separate database.
- **Support load:** support received 1,190 tickets and chat requests during the incident, roughly six times a normal Wednesday morning.
- **Data:** no data was lost, corrupted or exposed. We verified this by comparing invoice records against the write-ahead log for the whole incident window.

## 3. Timeline (all times UTC)

| Time | Event |
| --- | --- |
| 08:55 | A developer on the Exports team changes the rollout setting for `batch_export_v2` from "5 per cent of EU accounts" to what they believed was the same setting in the new flag dashboard. Because of a known display issue in the dashboard, the field labelled "percentage" was actually the field for "all accounts in region". The change is approved by a second developer through the normal review step. |
| 09:00 | The flag change takes effect. Batch export jobs scheduled for 09:00 start for all EU accounts that have exports scheduled. |
| 09:12 | Database connection usage on EU-1 reaches 200 of 200. First customer requests begin to time out. This is the start of customer impact. |
| 09:31 | An automated alert fires: "EU-1 API error rate above 5 per cent for 15 minutes." The on-call engineer (Site Reliability, primary on-call) acknowledges it at 09:33. Detection took 19 minutes from the start of impact. |
| 09:40 | The on-call engineer sees intermittent name-resolution errors in the logs and suspects a DNS problem with our cloud provider. Time is spent checking the provider status page and DNS configuration. |
| 10:05 | The DNS theory is ruled out: the name-resolution errors are a side effect of overloaded application servers, not the cause. The incident is raised to SEV-1 and an incident commander (Platform team lead) takes over. |
| 10:22 | A database engineer notices that most open connections belong to the batch export worker. |
| 10:41 | The incident commander asks the Exports team to switch off `batch_export_v2`. The flag is switched off at 10:44. |
| 10:44–11:20 | Connection usage does not fall as expected, because export jobs already running keep their connections until they finish or time out. The team decides not to kill running jobs, to avoid partially written export files. |
| 11:20 | The team lowers the job time-out for export workers from 60 minutes to 5 minutes as a temporary measure. Stuck jobs end and connections are released. |
| 11:42 | Connection usage on EU-1 falls below 120. Error rates return to normal. |
| 11:59 | Error rates and loading times have been normal for 15 minutes. The incident commander declares the end of customer impact. |
| 12:40 | The last delayed scheduled invoice email is sent. |
| 14:10 | Status page updated to "resolved"; customer email about delayed invoices sent. |

## 4. Root Cause

The root cause has two parts that only caused harm together.

First, the new batch export code had a defect: it opened a new database connection for every invoice in a batch, instead of using one connection for the whole batch. In testing, batches were small (at most 20 invoices) and the test database had a generous connection limit, so the defect was not visible. In production, some EU customers export batches of several thousand invoices on the first working days of the month.

Second, the flag was rolled out to 100 per cent of EU accounts instead of 5 per cent. The new flag dashboard, introduced in August, displayed the "all accounts in region" option in the position where the old dashboard showed the percentage field. The display issue was known to the team that built the dashboard and was listed in their backlog, but it had not been communicated to other teams. The reviewer of the change saw the same misleading screen and approved it.

At 5 per cent of accounts, the defect would most likely have caused higher connection use but not exhaustion, and would have been caught by the connection-usage dashboard during the normal rollout review.

We want to be clear that no individual is to blame. Both the developer and the reviewer followed the documented process. The process and the tools allowed a mistake that a person could reasonably make.

## 5. Why Detection and Recovery Took So Long

- **Alert threshold:** the alert required an error rate above 5 per cent for 15 minutes. There was no alert on connection-pool usage, which reached 100 per cent at 09:12 and would have pointed directly at the problem.
- **The DNS red herring:** overloaded application servers produced name-resolution errors in the logs, which looked like a DNS problem. About 25 minutes were spent on this theory.
- **Flag changes were not visible in the incident channel:** the flag change at 08:55 was recorded in the flag system's audit log, but nobody on the incident looked there until 10:22, because flag changes are not posted to the incident channel or the deployment log.
- **Running jobs kept their connections:** switching the flag off stopped new export jobs but did not release connections held by running ones. The 60-minute job time-out was much longer than necessary.

## 6. What Went Well

- No data was lost, and the team's decision not to kill running export jobs avoided corrupted export files.
- Scheduled invoices were queued and sent automatically after recovery; nothing was sent twice.
- The support team published a status page update within 12 minutes of the SEV-1 being declared and kept it updated every 30 minutes.
- The payment service, which uses a separate database, kept working throughout.

## 7. Action Items

| No. | Action | Owner (role) | Due date |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Fix the batch export code so that each batch uses a single database connection; add a test with a batch of 5,000 invoices against a database with a production-like connection limit. | Exports team lead | 19 September 2026 |
| 2 | Fix the flag dashboard display issue and require the rollout percentage to be typed out in a confirmation dialog for any change above 10 per cent. | Developer Tools team lead | 26 September 2026 |
| 3 | Add an alert when connection-pool usage on any primary database stays above 80 per cent for 3 minutes. | Site Reliability lead | 12 September 2026 |
| 4 | Post every feature flag change in production automatically to the deployment log and to any open incident channel. | Developer Tools team lead | 10 October 2026 |
| 5 | Reduce the default time-out for export jobs from 60 minutes to 15 minutes and document how to release connections held by running jobs safely. | Platform team lead | 3 October 2026 |

Progress on these items will be reviewed in the weekly reliability meeting until all are closed.

## 8. Lessons

1. **Roll out gradually, and make the rollout setting impossible to misread.** A gradual rollout is only a safety net if the tool shows the setting clearly.
2. **Alert on causes as well as symptoms.** An error-rate alert told us something was wrong; a connection-pool alert would have told us what.
3. **Make recent changes visible during incidents.** The question "what changed?" should be answerable in the incident channel within a minute.
4. **Test with production-like limits.** Connection limits, batch sizes and time-outs in test environments should match production for code that touches the database in bulk.

## 9. Communication to Customers

A short explanation was emailed to affected customers on 3 September at 14:10 UTC, and a public summary was posted on the status page. Customers on paid plans who were affected will receive a credit equal to one day of their subscription on their next bill, applied automatically.

## Appendix A: Glossary for Non-Engineers

- **Feature flag:** a switch that lets us turn a new feature on for some customers before turning it on for everyone.
- **Connection pool:** a fixed number of open lines between our application and the database. If all lines are busy, new requests must wait.
- **Time-out:** the maximum time a task is allowed to run or wait before it is stopped.
- **SEV-1:** our highest severity level, used when many customers cannot use a core feature.
- **Blameless review:** a review that looks at how systems and processes allowed a problem, rather than at who made a mistake.

*End of document.*

## 32. L6-04 (level 6: Long document summaries)

~~~~~~text
Summarise the key findings and limitations of the following study in at most 250 words. Then answer in one sentence: does it show that more sleep causes better exam results?

---

# Sleep, Study Habits and Exam Results: Findings from the 2026 Lindenfeld College Student Survey

*Synthetic document written for a blind benchmark. Lindenfeld College, its students, its staff and every figure in this report are fictional. Nothing here should be cited as real research.*

**Prepared by:** the Lindenfeld College Learning Support Unit
**Survey period:** 2 February to 1 March 2026
**Report date:** 15 May 2026

## Abstract

We surveyed first- and second-year students at Lindenfeld College about their sleep, study habits, part-time work and use of study techniques during the winter examination period, and linked their answers, with consent, to their average mark in the January examinations. Of 624 students invited, 212 completed the survey (a response rate of 34 per cent). Students who reported sleeping seven hours or more on a typical weeknight had a higher mean examination mark (71.3 out of 100) than students who reported sleeping less than seven hours (66.8). Students who reported using spaced repetition, reviewing material at increasing intervals, had a mean mark of 72.9, compared with 67.0 for those who did not. Students working more than 15 hours a week in paid jobs had lower marks on average. These are associations in a small, self-selected sample, measured mostly by self-report. They do not show that more sleep or a particular study technique causes better results, and we caution readers against interpreting them that way.

## 1. Background

The Learning Support Unit runs workshops on study skills and wellbeing for around 1,200 students each year. Staff and students often ask which habits are most associated with doing well in examinations. The published research literature contains many studies on sleep and learning, on spaced repetition and on the effects of paid work during studies, but we wanted to understand the situation of our own students, who are mostly the first in their family to attend higher education and who often combine study with paid work and caring responsibilities.

The aim of this survey was descriptive: to find out what our students actually do, and to see whether the patterns reported elsewhere are visible in our own data. It was not designed to test any intervention.

## 2. Method

### 2.1 Participants

All 624 first- and second-year students enrolled in the four departments of the college (Business, Health Sciences, Engineering Technology and Media) were invited by email to take part. Participation was voluntary and anonymous to the research team: a member of the registry staff not involved in the analysis matched survey responses to examination marks and then removed names and student numbers before the data were passed on.

212 students completed the survey, a response rate of 34 per cent. Respondents were 58 per cent women, 40 per cent men, and 2 per cent described their gender in another way or preferred not to say. Their median age was 21. Health Sciences students were over-represented (39 per cent of respondents, compared with 28 per cent of invited students) and Engineering Technology students were under-represented (14 per cent of respondents, compared with 25 per cent of invited students).

### 2.2 Survey

The online survey had 31 questions and took about twelve minutes to complete. It asked about:

- typical hours of sleep on weeknights and at weekends during the four weeks before the January examinations;
- the number of hours spent studying outside classes per week;
- which study techniques students used, chosen from a list with short descriptions (re-reading notes, highlighting, summarising, practice testing, spaced repetition, group study, and "other");
- hours of paid work per week;
- caring responsibilities;
- use of caffeine and energy drinks;
- a short wellbeing questionnaire.

All of these measures are self-reported. Students were asked to think back over the examination period, so their answers may be affected by memory and by what they think is the "right" answer.

### 2.3 Examination marks

The outcome was each student's average mark across all January examinations, on the college's 0–100 scale. Marks come from college records and are not self-reported.

### 2.4 Analysis

We compared mean marks between groups and calculated simple correlations. Because of the small sample, we did not attempt complex statistical models, and the differences reported below should be read as rough indications. Where we give a range, it is a 95 per cent confidence interval for the difference between group means.

## 3. Results

### 3.1 Sleep

On weeknights, 41 per cent of respondents (87 students) reported sleeping seven hours or more, and 59 per cent (125 students) reported sleeping less than seven hours. Only 9 per cent reported sleeping less than five hours.

| Weeknight sleep | Students | Mean exam mark |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 7 hours or more | 87 | 71.3 |
| Less than 7 hours | 125 | 66.8 |

The difference in means is 4.5 points (95 per cent confidence interval 1.2 to 7.8 points). Students who reported less sleep also reported more hours of paid work and more caffeine use, so the sleep groups differ in other ways too.

Weekend sleep showed no clear relationship with examination marks.

### 3.2 Study techniques

The most commonly reported techniques were re-reading notes (81 per cent) and highlighting (64 per cent). Practice testing was reported by 47 per cent of respondents and spaced repetition by 27 per cent (58 students).

| Technique reported | Students | Mean exam mark (users) | Mean exam mark (non-users) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Spaced repetition | 58 | 72.9 | 67.0 |
| Practice testing | 100 | 71.0 | 66.5 |
| Re-reading notes | 172 | 68.4 | 69.7 |
| Highlighting | 136 | 68.1 | 69.6 |

Students who used spaced repetition or practice testing had higher mean marks than those who did not. Re-reading and highlighting showed small differences in the other direction, which are well within what could be expected by chance in a sample of this size. Students who used spaced repetition were also more likely to be in their second year and to have attended one of our study-skills workshops, so it is not possible to separate the technique from these other factors.

### 3.3 Paid work

Overall, 63 per cent of respondents had a paid job during the examination period. Students working more than 15 hours a week (46 students) had a mean mark of 64.2, compared with 69.9 for students working 15 hours or fewer, including those not working at all. These students also reported less sleep on average.

### 3.4 Study time

Reported hours of study outside classes had only a weak positive correlation with examination marks (r = 0.18). Several students with high reported study hours had below-average marks, and several with modest study hours had high marks. How students studied seemed to matter at least as much as how long.

### 3.5 Caffeine and wellbeing

Students who reported drinking three or more energy drinks a week reported lower wellbeing scores and less sleep. We found no clear relationship between caffeine use and examination marks once sleep was taken into account, but the sample is too small to say this with confidence.

## 4. Discussion

The patterns in our data are broadly similar to those described in the published literature: students who reported more sleep, and students who used active study techniques such as spaced repetition and practice testing, had higher examination marks on average. Heavy paid work was associated with lower marks.

However, our survey **cannot show cause and effect**. There are several reasons for caution:

1. **Self-selection.** Only about one in three invited students responded. Students who respond to a survey about study habits may be more organised, or more interested in their studies, than those who do not.
2. **Self-report.** Sleep, study hours and techniques were reported by students themselves, looking back over several weeks. People often overestimate their sleep and study time.
3. **Confounding.** The groups we compared differ in many ways at once. Students who sleep less also work more hours and drink more caffeine; students who use spaced repetition are more often in their second year and have more often attended a workshop. Any of these could explain part of the differences in marks.
4. **Small sample and uneven representation.** With 212 respondents, and with some departments over- or under-represented, the estimates are imprecise and may not apply to the college as a whole.
5. **Reverse direction.** It is possible that students who were already doing well felt less stressed and therefore slept better, rather than sleep improving their results.

For these reasons, we do not recommend presenting these figures to students as evidence that changing one habit will raise their marks by a particular number of points.

## 5. Recommendations

Despite these limits, the findings are consistent with existing evidence and support some practical steps:

1. **Continue and expand the study-skills workshops**, with more emphasis on practice testing and spaced repetition, which fewer than half of students currently use.
2. **Include sleep in wellbeing guidance during examination periods**, presented as general good practice rather than as a guaranteed way to raise marks.
3. **Work with the careers and finance offices** to help students who need to work long hours find more flexible jobs, or to identify hardship funding.
4. **Run a better-designed follow-up.** A future study should invite a random sample of students with follow-up reminders to raise the response rate, use sleep diaries rather than memory, and, if resources allow, test a workshop programme by comparing students who are offered it with students who are offered it later.

## 6. Ethics and Data Protection

The survey was approved by the college's research ethics committee. Participation was voluntary, and students could withdraw at any point before submitting. Linking to examination marks was done only for students who gave explicit consent. The research team never saw names or student numbers. Data will be deleted three years after publication of this report.

## Acknowledgements

We thank the 212 students who took part, the registry staff who carried out the data linking, and the student union, which helped us word the questions.

*End of report.*

## 33. L6-05 (level 6: Long document summaries)

~~~~~~text
Summarise the plot of the following short story in at most 150 words. Name the main characters, the central conflict and how it ends.

---

# The Lighthouse Keeper's Ledger

*Synthetic short story written for a blind benchmark. All characters and places are fictional.*

Maren Holt had kept the light on Skerra Point for nineteen years, and in all that time the ledger had never lied to her.

It lived on the shelf above the oil store, a long book bound in green cloth that had gone grey at the corners. Every delivery went into it: the date, the supply boat, the number of drums, the weight of each drum, the signature of whoever had carried them up the slipway. Every night's burning went into it too, measured off the gauge on the big tank in the lamp room. The two columns, what came in and what went out, were supposed to meet at the end of every month like two ends of a rope. For nineteen years they had.

In the autumn of the year the harbour board changed the tenders, they stopped meeting.

The first month the gap was small enough to be a mistake: eleven litres, which she put down to a sticky gauge. The second month it was forty. The third month, after the October delivery, it was ninety-two litres, nearly half a drum, and Maren sat at the kitchen table with the ledger open and the lamp turned low and felt something cold settle in her stomach.

There were only three people who came and went from Skerra Point. There was Maren herself. There was her nephew Tobias, fifteen years old, sent out from the mainland in September after his mother's illness, who spent his days doing correspondence lessons at the same kitchen table and his evenings on the rocks with a fishing line. And there was Idris Vale, who ran the supply boat *Curlew* out from Harrow Quay every second Thursday with oil, flour, post and whatever else the board decided the light needed.

She did not want it to be Tobias. She told herself that was not a reason to think it wasn't.

---

She watched the next delivery from the lamp gallery, where she could see the slipway without being seen. Idris brought the *Curlew* in neatly on the rising tide, as he always did. He was a broad, quiet man in his sixties with a grey beard and hands like coiled rope, and he had run the island routes for longer than Maren had kept the light. He and Tobias rolled six drums up the slipway on the trolley, one at a time, and stacked them in the oil store. Idris signed the ledger in his square capitals. Six drums, two hundred litres each.

When the *Curlew* had gone, Maren went down with the dipstick and measured each drum. Five were full. The sixth was short by sixty litres, and the seal on its cap had been cut and pressed back so carefully that she had to hold it to the light to see it.

So it was Idris. The thought did not bring her any relief. Idris had pulled her brother out of the water off Harrow Head twenty years ago. Idris had brought medicine across in the January storm when Tobias's grandmother was dying on the island. If Idris Vale was stealing oil from the light, there had to be a reason, and she was afraid of what it would be.

---

She said nothing to Tobias. But Tobias, it turned out, had been watching her watching.

"You measured the drums," he said that evening, not looking up from his algebra. "After the boat."

"I measure everything."

"Not usually after the boat. Usually on Sunday." He put his pencil down. "Is something wrong with the oil?"

She considered lying to him and found she was too tired. She showed him the ledger, the two columns that did not meet, the cut seal.

Tobias looked at the numbers for a long time. Then he said, "Mr Vale's been taking drums off at Corrie."

Corrie was the small island two miles south, with a school of nine children, a chapel and a harbour too shallow for anything bigger than the *Curlew*. The supply boat called there on the way back to Harrow Quay.

"How do you know that?"

"I go fishing off the north rocks. You can see Corrie harbour from there with your binoculars." He had the decency to look embarrassed about the binoculars. "He stops at the school landing, not the harbour. He carries something heavy up. Twice I've seen it."

---

Maren took the dinghy across to Corrie the next Saturday, on the pretext of buying eggs.

The schoolhouse was a single room with a stove at one end and nine desks at the other, and it was warm. That was the first thing she noticed: warm, in November, on an island where the coal boat had not called since the end of August. The teacher, a young woman named Ailsa Brennan who had come out from the mainland the previous year, made her tea on a small paraffin heater at the back of the room, and Maren saw a drum standing against the wall behind the stove with the board's stencil on its side.

She did not have to ask. Ailsa saw her looking and went pale, and then, being honest, told her everything. The board had cut the coal allowance for the Corrie school when the tenders changed, on the grounds that nine children were too few to justify a delivery. Ailsa had written three letters and received one reply, saying that the matter was under review. By October the children were doing their lessons in coats and gloves, and two of the youngest had been ill for weeks. Idris, who had five grandchildren in that school, had started bringing a few litres from each delivery to the light. He had paid for a converter for the stove out of his own pocket.

"He said the light wouldn't miss it," Ailsa said. "He said you kept so much in reserve."

That was true, as far as it went. Maren kept a reserve because of the winter storms, when the *Curlew* could not cross for weeks at a time.

---

The storm came in the second week of December.

It came faster than the forecast said, a south-westerly that built through the afternoon until the spray was coming over the top of the lamp gallery. The *Curlew* was due that Thursday and did not come. By the evening the wind had reached a strength Maren had seen only twice before, and at nine o'clock the main light went out.

It was not the oil. It was the burner, a cracked fitting on the vaporiser that she had been nursing since the summer. She had a spare, but fitting it meant shutting off the supply, draining the line and working by torchlight in a lamp room that was shaking with every gust. It would take forty minutes if nothing went wrong. Somewhere out in the dark, ships would be looking for the light on Skerra Point to find the channel between the Point and the Corrie reef.

"What do I do?" said Tobias, white-faced in the doorway.

"The emergency lamp. On the gallery. You light it and you keep it lit, whatever happens, until I tell you."

The emergency lamp was a big old paraffin lantern, much weaker than the main light but enough to mark the Point. It burned from its own small tank. Tobias lit it with shaking hands on the third try and then stood beside it on the open gallery with a rope tied round his waist, shielding it from the gusts with his body, for an hour and ten minutes, while Maren worked on the burner below him with blood running from a cut on her thumb.

The main light came back at ten past ten. At twenty past, through the rain, Maren saw the lights of a coaster passing safely through the channel, much closer to the reef than she would have liked.

The emergency lamp's tank was nearly empty when Tobias came in. It had held enough paraffin for about ninety minutes.

"If it had been longer," he said, and did not finish.

"If it had been longer," said Maren, "we'd have needed the reserve."

They both knew how much of the reserve had gone to Corrie.

---

Idris came out three days later, when the sea had calmed. He knew as soon as he saw Maren's face. He sat down at the kitchen table, in front of the ledger, and put his big hands flat on the cloth cover.

"I'd do it again," he said. "I'm sorry for the lying. I'm not sorry for the children."

"I know," said Maren. "I'd do it again too, probably. But the light can't be what pays for the board's mistakes, Idris. Not with the reserve. Not in December."

They talked for a long time. Tobias, who was supposed to be doing his algebra, listened to every word.

In the end, it was Tobias who suggested what they did. Maren wrote the missing oil into the ledger, every litre of it, in a new line under the October and November entries: *Lent to Corrie School for heating, by agreement of the keeper, to be repaid.* She signed it, and Idris signed it under her name in his square capitals. Then the three of them wrote a letter to the harbour board, and Ailsa Brennan added a page, and the nine children of Corrie school each signed it too, some of them in crayon. The letter set out what had happened, the cut coal allowance, the cold classroom, the oil, the storm and the forty minutes of darkness on Skerra Point. It asked the board to restore the school's heating allowance and to replace the oil lent from the light's reserve.

Maren did not know whether the board would answer. She did not know whether she would still have a job when it did. But when she put the ledger back on the shelf above the oil store, for the first time in three months, the two columns met.

*The end.*
